headline_insight: While Health Insurance dominates coverage for both genders, female clients report significantly higher expectations of extra credit life benefits—such as medical and weather assistance—compared to male clients, highlighting a critical need for targeted product education.
paragraphs: Health insurance represents the primary coverage type for both genders, held by 75.1% of female clients (n=1,140) and 90.8% of male clients (n=532), followed by Enhanced Credit Life (16.6% of females, n=252; 5.6% of males, n=33) and Crop Insurance (8.3% of females, n=126; 3.6% of males, n=21). Across the robust country samples, Net Promoter Scores (NPS) vary widely, with Kenya achieving the highest score of 36.2 (n=265) and Tanzania reporting a negative NPS of -10.3 (n=272). Because qualitative client voice quotes and external benchmark data are not available for these indicators, these quantitative metrics serve as our primary baseline. For the Latin America and Caribbean region—including Bolivia (n=1), Dominican Republic (n=1), Ecuador (n=1), Mexico (n=5), and Honduras (n=1)—the extremely small sample sizes fail the minimum-n threshold, meaning their highly polarized NPS results must be treated as purely directional and illustrative rather than statistically robust.

A key programming implication emerges from a statistically significant gender divergence in clients' understanding of credit life insurance. Female clients are significantly more likely than male clients to believe that credit life products include extra benefits, with 15.7% of females versus 5.3% of males expecting help with medical costs, 5.3% of females versus 0.9% of males expecting weather-related crop assistance, and 8.2% of females versus 2.7% of males expecting help for damaged business assets (all significant at p_adj = 0.0). Meanwhile, for Health Insurance, only 14.8% of females and 17.9% of males report that medical care has actually become easier, and 21.4% of females and 24.2% of males report no change in out-of-pocket costs. This gap suggests that VisionFund must proactively clarify product boundaries to prevent misconceptions, particularly among female clients, while simultaneously working to enhance the tangible value and accessibility of its core health insurance offerings.

For Crop Insurance, the findings are heavily concentrated in Vietnam (where the overall country sample is n=147, but the gender-disaggregated crop insurance cuts have n_ok=false with 126 females and 21 males) and must be treated as directional rather than statistically robust. Directionally, 47.6% of female crop insurance clients reported that their farming approach slightly improved compared to 28.6% of males, yet 61.1% of females and 66.7% of males reported that they only recovered from agricultural shocks after more than three months. Furthermore, 32.5% of females and 38.1% of males definitely plan to renew their crop insurance at full premium, while 11.9% of females and 4.8% of males probably would not renew. These illustrative findings suggest that while agricultural insurance shows promise in altering farming behaviors positively, especially for women, VisionFund needs to refine the product design to accelerate post-shock recovery times and secure long-term renewal rates.
